Why React

What React gives you

Components

Build a button, card or navbar once and reuse it everywhere.

Auto updates

Change the data, and React updates the page for you. No manual DOM code.

Huge community

Used by Meta, Netflix, Airbnb and most job adverts. Tons of help online.

slides.title: A new project with Vite
slides.html:
Setup

A new project with Vite

  • Vite creates a React project in seconds
  • npm run dev starts a local server with live reload
  • Your code lives in src/
  • App.jsx is where you start

Terminal

npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
 
# open http://localhost:5173
 
my-app/
  index.html
  src/
    main.jsx   # puts <App /> on the page
    App.jsx    # your first component

slides.title: Components and JSX
slides.html:
Components

Components and JSX

  • A component is a function that returns JSX
  • JSX looks like HTML inside JavaScript
  • Names start with a capital letter
  • Use className, not class
  • Return one parent element (or <>…</>)

App.jsx

function Header() {
  return (
    <header className="header">
      <h1>BlockHub</h1>
      <p>Learn. Build. Grow.</p>
    </header>
  );
}
 
export default function App() {
  return <Header />;
}

slides.title: Putting JavaScript in JSX
slides.html:
Components

Putting JavaScript in JSX

  • Curly braces { } run JavaScript inside JSX
  • Use them for variables, maths and function calls
  • Styles are objects: style={{ color: "green" }}

Profile.jsx

export default function Profile() {
  const name = "Ada";
  const lessons = 12;
 
  return (
    <div className="card">
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>{lessons * 2} hours of learning</p>
      <p>Joined {new Date().getFullYear()}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

slides.title: Passing data with props
slides.html:
Props

Passing data with props

  • Props are inputs to a component
  • Pass them like HTML attributes
  • Read them in the function's parameters
  • Same component, different data

CourseCard.jsx

function CourseCard({ title, weeks }) {
  return (
    <div className="card">
      <h3>{title}</h3>
      <p>{weeks} weeks</p>
    </div>
  );
}
 
<CourseCard title="Full-Stack" weeks={10} />
<CourseCard title="Backend" weeks={10} />

slides.title: State is data that changes. When it changes, React re-draws.
slides.html:
State

State is data that changes. When it changes, React re-draws.

Props come from the parent. State lives inside the component and changes over time: a counter, a form input, a list of tasks.

Full-Stack Development · Week 3 · Introduction to React

10

slides.title: Managing state with useState
slides.html:
State

Managing state with useState

  • useState gives you a value and a setter
  • Call the setter to change it
  • Never change state directly
  • React updates the screen for you

Counter.jsx

import { useState } from "react";
 
export default function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
 
  return (
    <div>
      <p>You clicked {count} times</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
        Click me
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

slides.title: Handling events
slides.html:
Events

Handling events

  • onClick, onChange, onSubmit (camelCase)
  • Pass a function, don't call it: onClick={handle}
  • For inputs, keep the value in state

Greeting.jsx

export default function Greeting() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
 
  const handleChange = (e) => setName(e.target.value);
 
  return (
    <div>
      <input value={name} onChange={handleChange} />
      <p>Hello, {name || "stranger"}!</p>
    </div>
  );
}

slides.title: Conditional rendering
slides.html:
Rendering

Conditional rendering

  • Show different things based on state
  • &&: show it only if true
  • ? :: choose between two things

Login.jsx

export default function Login() {
  const [loggedIn, setLoggedIn] = useState(false);
 
  return (
    <div>
      {loggedIn ? <p>Welcome back!</p> : <p>Please log in</p>}
 
      {loggedIn && <button>View dashboard</button>}
 
      <button onClick={() => setLoggedIn(!loggedIn)}>
        {loggedIn ? "Log out" : "Log in"}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

slides.title: Rendering lists with keys
slides.html:
Rendering

Rendering lists with keys

  • Use map to turn an array into elements
  • Every item needs a unique key
  • Use an id, not the array index, when you can

TrackList.jsx

const tracks = [
  { id: 1, name: "Full-Stack" },
  { id: 2, name: "Backend" },
  { id: 3, name: "Design" },
];
 
export default function TrackList() {
  return (
    <ul>
      {tracks.map((t) => (
        <li key={t.id}>{t.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

slides.title: The components
slides.html:
Build · step 1

The components

  • Each component in its own file
  • Pass data down with props
  • Keep state where it changes

// SkillList.jsx
export default function SkillList({ skills }) {
  return (
    <ul className="skills">
      {skills.map((s) => <li key={s}>{s}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}
 
// LikeButton.jsx
export default function LikeButton() {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>
      ❤️ {likes} {likes >= 10 && "You're popular!"}
    </button>
  );
}
